title: Think Differently Innovation Toolkit Problem solving with your team 9.23.21

cues.text: >> Like to thank everyone for joining today's DAU webcast,
another episode of the Think Differently Series.
This one is problem solving with your team.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event, and we also have our host on, Dr. Marina Theodotou.
The agenda's posted.
Your microphones will be muted throughout the session.
This session is being recorded, and will be posted to dau.edu/dau-webcasts.
Please submit your questions via the chat.
If you haven't found the chat icon, it's in a little circle
with an arrow pointing out of it at the bottom.
There will be a survey at the end.
We do appreciate your feedback.
It helps us to curate new events.
If you're here for CLPs, this session does qualify for up
to 1.5 CLP with supervisor approval.
They are not automatic.
You will need to apply for them.
A lot of people take a screenshot of the event with your name in it as the attendance,
or a screenshot of the survey at the end.
And now, I'm going to turn it over to Marina to introduce our speakers.
>> Thank you so much, Emmett.
It's a pleasure to be here again.
It is episode 18 of Think Differently.
We're super excited that you were able to join us.
For those of you that are joining for the first time, welcome.
My name is Marina Theodotou, and I am, as Emmett mentioned --
I'm the host and curator of the event.
And as background, the Think Differently Series -- we created it as a platform,
to create a platform that would inspire and empower you to get involved and engaged
in conversations around topics that are critical
to the national defense strategy, and to you in your jobs.
So today, we're super excited to welcome members of the innovation team at MITRE, and with that,
I would like to welcome Casey Creech, who is an innovator at MITRE.
And he tells us that when a team forms and starts working with executive leadership,
the gap between what we do and what's actually possible breaks progress.
And Casey fills the gap between the ideas and the execution by building teams designed
around positivity, creativity, and fun.
Casey is a Navy nuclear-trained submarine officer, accredited facilitator,
graphic designer, and executive leadership coach.
He often serves as a guide for teams to reveal invisible opportunities
and challenges, not just the obvious ones.
Casey, welcome.
It's a pleasure to have you here.
>> Oh, fabulous, and I look forward to chatting, and seeing where we can take this,
as there's some amazing people you've assembled here.
I'm just honored to be in the room with the rest of the members of this team here.
>> Thank you, absolutely.
Next, we'd like to welcome Karim Thompson, senior geospatial computing engineer at MITRE.
Karim's day job involves the analysis of location to uncover hidden patterns,
improve predictive modeling, and create a competitive advantage across multiple domains.
However, given Karim's interests outside geospatial science,
such as relationship building and strategic planning,
he sought out an additional opportunity.
So he became a trained innovation facilitator who helps teams work together more effectively
and deliver novel solutions to difficult problems.
Karim, so great to have you with us.
Thank you, and welcome.
>> Thank you, and kudos to your team for uploading
that picture we took this morning to the slide deck [laughter].
>> Thanks, Karim.
All right, next, we'd like to welcome Dan Ward innovation catalyst at MITRE as well.
Dan is an innovation catalyst that previously served more than 20 years as an officer
in the U.S. Air Force, where he specialized in leading small, high-speed,
low-cost technology development programs.
Dan is a prolific author of three books, "LIFT," "The Simplicity Cycle," and "F.I.R.E."
Super-exciting to have you with us, Dan.
Welcome.
>> Hey, thanks.
It's great to be here.
Again, thank you for the opportunity, and for sharing this audience with our team.
And I should put in a quick plug for a new book coming out.
It's called "To Boldly Go," comes out September 30th, leadership lessons from science fiction.
Check it out wherever books are sold.
>> Fantastic.
Thank you.
As a disclaimer, DAU cannot endorse any books, but we're sharing them
as learning opportunities and learning assets.
So with that, thank you, and let's move to Josh LeFevre, strategic futures designer at MITRE.
He helps bridge data-driven and human-driven innovation efforts,
and he empowers the development
of future omni-channel human-centered products and services.
Josh, great to have you with us.
Welcome.
>> Thank you for having me.
>> Fantastic.
And next, we have Tracey Amos, enterprise engineer principle at MITRE,
who has led strategic and business transformation projects
across multiple federal agencies, and has extensive experience
in translating broad strategic vision into practical, executable steps.
Tracey holds an MBA from Wharton School of Business and a bachelor of arts from the College
of Arts and Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.
Tracey, great to have you with us.
Thank you for joining us.
>> Thank you.
Great to be here today.
Looking forward to the conversation.
>> Fantastic.
And last but not least, Gabby Raymond, who is a cyber deception
and adversary engagement specialist expert at MITRE.
She holds a B.S in mathematics and computer science, and an M.S. in computer science
from Tufts, and her research has spanned topics in intrusion detection, cyber-physical systems,
and machine learning applications for security.
Gabby recently co-authored a Choose Your Own Adventure-style book called "The Toolbox
of Innovation" with members of MITRE's innovation toolkit team.
And outside of work, she enjoys knitting and judging science fairs.
Gabby is the co-capability area lead for the cyber deception
and adversary engagement at MITRE.
Gabby, great to have you with us.
Welcome.
>> Thank you for the introduction, Marina.
>> Fantastic.
All right.
So let's get started.
So this conversation came together because, as you probably know, I'm very active on LinkedIn,
and I saw this post by Dan about the innovation toolkit.
And when I saw it, I thought about all the different teams that are doing innovation
around the DoD, and the national security ecosystem.
And I thought, my goodness, would be wonderful to have members of the team to come
to Think Differently and talk about this toolkit, what it is, and why did you create it.
So, Dan, welcome again.
We're going to start with you.
So help us set the stage.
So why did your team create this toolkit, and what is it?
And how can we use it?
>> Absolutely.
Great question, and thanks again for the opportunity to be here.
You know, it's interesting.
We built this toolkit to use it, to use it in our own work, to solve our own problems,
to use it with our teams and our projects.
And I think, you know, we find that the best tools and products tend to come that way.
You know, you write the book you want to read.
You sing the song -- you write the song you want to sing.
You make the tool that you want to use.
And so, that was very much the roots of this,
is we just saw the need for the type of work that we do.
These types of tools would be helpful.
We did a great big survey of, like, 300 tools out there in kind of the --
in the world, and we cherry-picked a couple of the favorites, and then made a bunch of our own,
and kind of put them together into this toolkit that was primarily for our own use.
And what do you know?
We discovered that it worked pretty well for the projects that we're doing,
and then it ended up being something that was shareable, too.
So what is it?
The innovation toolkit is a collection of about two dozen, slightly over, tools, and techniques,
and methods that I think Karim's bio mentioned it or explained it pretty well.
These are designed to help people work together,
help them deliver innovative solutions to hard problems.
That's what they're really all about, to help us build clarity and consensus
around what the problem is, to help us simplify our processes, our system architectures,
our organizational structures, our communication products, and then to help us, like,
not just get clarity and consensus, but then to take action.
And then, at the end of it, to tell the story of what is it we're trying to do,
what did we attempt, what did we accomplish, and it's very practitioner-oriented tools.
Again, because we built them for ourselves as engineers, and coders,
and cybersecurity specialists, geospatial intelligence folks, and as practitioners,
and although a lot of us have a DoD background,
we found it getting pretty widely adopted in the health space as well.
So it's been fascinating to see how wisely these things have been adopted.
So looking forward to filling in a lot more detail as the conversation goes,
but that's a quick summary of why we did it, and kind of what it is.
>> I love that, because you started with the "why," just as we think about how Simon Cynic --
us, to start with why, and then the "how," and then the "what."
And so, it sounds like the "why" was, you needed -- why do you need this?
Well, we need it so that we can be more effective in our job, and then from there,
you extrapolated and said, "Well, why don't we share it with the rest
of the world, so that they can also benefit?"
So that's a great segue to Tracey, because your efforts have been focusing
on breaking these big challenges into practical and executable steps.
So how does the toolkit, like, help address these challenges,
and can you expand a little bit of how do you go about breaking these big,
insurmountable challenges into smaller steps that are more easy, essentially,
for people to understand and embrace?
Tracey -- you.
>> Yes, thank you so much for the question.
Interesting enough, the toolkit contains several tools that can really help attain at the outset
of making sure that they're defining and solving the right problem.
There's a problem-framing tool that allows a team, at the outset,
and then periodically throughout the work that the team is doing, to really make sure
that they're exploring the problem space, that they are formulating a robust problem statement,
ultimately to decide that they are, in fact, going to be solving the right problem.
Oftentimes, a team comes together, and you think you have a sense of the problem.
But as you explore, and question, and challenge more, you get to understand
and really zero in on the problem to be solved.
So really like to utilize that tool, particularly at the outset,
to dissect the problem, to ask questions, and if you look at the tool that's available
on our public-facing website, it has a series of questions in the question bank
that really force the team to think about the problem through different lens.
Another tool that I like to use at the outset of thinking about a problem
that we've come together to solve is called our premortem tool,
and that's a tool where you take the team on an imaginary journey,
where you look at what does it look like if you fail to solve this problem.
And by understanding what failure looks like, it gives you an opportunity to think about and plan
for risk mitigation, to get the team aligned around what does success look
like from an outcomes perspective.
So those are just a couple of the tools.
There's so many more that I could elaborate on that we use throughout the process as a team,
but I know we're going to touch on some of those as my colleagues share perspectives.
>> Fantastic.
Thanks, Tracey, and actually, this is wonderful.
Because as you were speaking, your colleagues have been adding the tools in the chat.
So this is wonderful, because we want the audience to be able to click.
Thanks, Dan and Casey, and other team members that are highlighting the tools.
So problem framing is critical, and also premortem.
We hear a lot about postmortem, so the hot wash type of exercise,
but premortem is quite interesting.
Because you -- it puts you in almost like a little bit of a morbid mindset of what happens
if this doesn't work out, and then you can work backwards from there, and figure out how
to actually ensure you're preventing those negative outcomes, right?
And so, Casey, this is a great segue, because you mentioned that this was your favorite tool.
Actually, you couldn't pick, Casey.
You can't pick which one is your favorite tool.
So you mentioned, as we heard in your bio, that you ask new questions.
In my mind, innovators -- as innovators, we ask new questions of old problems,
and you ask two very critical questions.
What could we do, and what's actually possible?
And there's usually that gap.
Can you discuss that a little bit more, and help us understand -- how do you close the gap?
>> That's -- you know, everybody's crazy busy here, right?
And when I'm done talking, some people will be scratching their head, wondering what I said,
and you might even be thinking that I haven't thought this through thoroughly.
You might even see me putting a soapbox down, standing up
and trying to chant out to the world.
There's a gap that often -- obviously, that exists between what you can do,
which is often what you do, and what's possible.
And as I think through this, there's probably two things that stand out to me most
when it comes to addressing that gap, is that you're most likely
to miss what you're never looking for, and the indirect path
to innovation is almost always the right path to choose over the direct route.
And Marina, talking to you earlier today, it kind of sounded
like you took a very indirect route to grow the attendees
to these sessions, and it kind of started slow.
And then it ramped off, and that's the way most innovation efforts go.
And so, let's break those two things down.
You're going to miss what you're not looking for,
and the indirect route's always the right route to take.
When you look at Peter Drucker and his seminal work on innovation and entrepreneurship,
he kind of lays out seven things that get you to innovation.
On one end is, let's go through and make lightning strike.
On the other end, it's like, oh, lightning struck.
What can we do with that?
And he says the surprise is often where you're most likely to be successful with innovating.
In other words, you don't know what's going to happen, so how do you create an environment
where things can happen you aren't expecting?
So let's look at that gap again, that gap that exists between what we can do,
and that gap that exists between what's possible.
You might even think about the gap between what fails and what works, and you might even think
about the gap between what makes sense and what's weird.
And if you draw an x-y axis, and say the x-y axis -- we got works and fails on one side,
and we got makes sense and is weird on the other side.
The innovation space often happens in that it's kind of weird space, and by exploring that kind
of weird space, you ultimately get to something that just might work.
So when you look at the innovation, the question was --
this is about innovation, about thinking differently.
When you strip away innovation, and you think about what it is,
it's actually altering reality, right?
It's taking something that seems like it's weird,
and moving it up to, oh, that makes sense.
And the ITK toolkit and other tools that Dan explored --
you know, there's so many great ones out there.
And how do you focus down and build something you like using?
A lot of these tools are intended to get to the hidden and invisible opportunities
and challenges, not just the obvious ones.
So how do you spend more space in that invisible and hidden area to pull
out some things that really stand out to you?
So that's kind of the first thing I think about, when I think about that you're always going
to miss what you're not looking for.
And when you take an indirect route, it's always the right route to take.
I like to think about going cross-country, right?
You start on the east coast.
You got to go to the west coast, and at some point, you come to a raging river.
And I think instinctively, you know, when you see a raging river, you don't go straight --
you don't go right across the ford right there.
You don't try to go across right there.
Instinctively, we know to explore up and down the river to try
to find a place that's easier to cross.
What we don't often think about doing is like, hey, let's stop our journey here, create a bed
and breakfast, and serve the best old-fashioned on the west coast.
So how do you go through and explore more opportunity in that space?
And here's a quick tip to -- a quick tool I think the audience can walk away with,
and use at the next meeting.
It's a tool to get to the hidden and the invisible opportunities and challenges
that exist, a tool to help elevate your innovation game, a tool to --
that's actually backed up by something in the "sounds weird,
but works" category, you know, behavioral science.
There's this wonderful thing called anchoring bias,
and anchoring bias is a beautiful thing, right?
Because as humans, we tend to follow the first thing that someone says, and it's amazing--
when the highest-paid person in the room speaks,
we tend to align around that highest-paid person's side of the room.
So how do we, as a group, go through when an idea, opportunity, or challenge emerges --
how can we go through in that moment and actually capture the ideas
that aren't influenced by anchoring bias?
So here's a tip.
Next time you bring your team together, and you're working through team,
and you have an idea, or an opportunity, or a challenge,
ask the team to collectively put all their thoughts to how to address it.
And have the entire team submit their ideas at the same time.
Post-It notes are a good example.
A shared Word document's another example, and you can even do it with e-mail,
with a delayed e-mail response, where you ask everybody
to send their response in at 1600 on Tuesday.
And the beautiful thing about this is, when everybody's got all their thoughts on paper,
once all those ideas exist in one space, ask everybody to read what everybody else posted.
Then ask them to go through and vote on the ideas,
and have a discussion about where the vote lies.
You might find the group's lining in one position.
You might also find there's an outlier over here who thinks differently from everybody else,
and they might be the person to go forward.
So the technique's basically called vote first, then discuss.
And the next time you have an event with your team,
try to vote first before you discuss the ideas.
So I guess to kind of summarize up your thought, you talked about how do you address that gap
between what can be and what's possible.
I think there's two things.
Always look for things that you might not be looking for, and take the indirect route.
Oh, and something I'll talk to Emmett -- I'll post something in chat here.
It's a quick one-minute video.
I think it's one minute and eight seconds.
It's an awareness test, and I"d ask you to watch the ball being passed back
and forth with the team in white shirts.
And it might change the way you think about the world.
It did for me.
So that's kind of me -- I'll put my soapbox aside now.
So two things -- you're always going to miss what you're not looking for,
and the indirect route is always the right route to take when you're doing innovation.
>> I love that.
Thank you so much, Casey, for analyzing that for us, and giving us those two things
to remember, which we put in the chat.
I'm wondering -- is the video the one with the gorilla that passes --
>> Oh, no, don't say that.
Don't say that.
>> -- okay [laughter].
>> No [laughter].
One thing I should've said is, don't listen to any of the comments.
Just watch the video.
>> Oh, okay.
Don't listen to any of the comments.
Just watch the video.
>> Don't listen to any comments.
Just watch the ball being passed back and forth.
>> Clearly, we have a number of innovators who are thinking and doing things differently here,
and I love the maxim of, you know, the indirect path, the indirect path to innovation.
So it's a little bit like, go where there's no path, and leave a trail.
And Gabby, we'll come to you, because a lot of these maxims are great to collate
and distill into books for innovators.
I know there are many books out there, and you were involved
in writing the toolbox of innovation.
So there you go.
Again, this is not an endorsement, but it is a sharing of a learning asset.
So this -- we're doing all this in the construct of learning.
And so, Gabby, tell us a little bit about the book-writing experience,
and what did you guys include in that book?
I haven't read it, so I'm looking forward to reading it.
But how did you keep the innovator in mind as you were writing?
>> Yeah, so I'll talk a little bit about how we landed on the choice
of a Choose Your Own Adventure book.
So a small subset of the group were like, hey, what would it look like if we wrote a book
to capture the spirit of the tools that we have in innovation toolkit?
And we tossed a whole bunch of different ideas around to say,
you know, what would that book look like?
And one idea was tossed out of a Choose Your Own Adventure book.
And we just thought that that was so fun and so playful,
and something that we're all really interested in working on.
So the book goes through -- you know, the reader is popped into this fictional situation,
which is left abstract enough that you can kind of plug in your own details of the projects
that you're working on, or your own workplace, plus a set of characters that we put together,
that we thought would help guide the reader through the different scenarios
and different situations, where they can choose to use one tool, or another tool,
or chain together multiple tools.
And so, our team just had a lot of fun.
We didn't have any specific leader, so this is a really unique experience for me,
because I'm used to having one person who's in charge,
who dictates what everyone else is going to do on the project.
And this was very organic.
You know, we wrote the scenes that we wanted to write,
and one of my favorite parts was stringing together this whole spaghetti mess
of the different scenes that we had, and which pathways we could connect through the book.
It was a little bit of a nightmare, but also, it can together so well that I'm just really proud
of the book that we've put together.
And so, I encourage everyone to get a copy of it.
Plus, like, being the author, I want more people to read it, and appreciate the work
that our entire team put into this.
But I think it's a fun, playful opportunity to explore the different tools that we have,
and apply that to your own situations.
>> Fantastic.
That sounds so exciting.
As you were speaking, I was thinking about, yeah, the organic process.
You almost crowd-sourced all this wisdom, and you put together the book.
And Victoria Cordova [assumed spelling] says, "The fire-eating author -- what?
I read the section about the author, so interesting.
I will download and read.
Thank you."
So folks are already reacting, and Dan says, "If you're going to write a book
with seven co-authors, a Choose Your Own Adventure format provides a lot of flexibility
for various voices, and ideas, and autonomy."
So that's fantastic.
So innovating your way into writing a book -- so you guys not only are creating innovative tools,
but you're also applying them, sounds like, in delivering learning for the rest of us.
And this brings us to Karim.
You're a geospatial engineer, and you're also an innovation facilitator.
And you talked a little bit about that, about wanting to have a new experience.
So can you walk us through the journey and mission to --
and your mission to help innovation teams?
Because I think a lot of people in our audience are -- they have their day job,
and then they have this innovation passion.
And by sharing your perspective, we can learn a little bit
about how do you pursue that journey and have both.
You don't have to choose.
You can have this and that.
Karim, over to you.
>> Yes, thank you, Marina.
So I didn't set out to be an innovator.
In fact, I don't think we have defined innovation yet.
I know I've heard Dan define it as innovation equals novelty plus impact,
and I like that definition.
Because I consider that something is novel and impactful, depending on the audience,
from that person's -- you take the person's perspective, the stakeholder's perspective
to determine whether something is novel, or impactful, or him or her.
With regards to my journey, again, I'm in the habit of describing kind of my interests
and skills as an intersection of three domains.
So if you consider, like, a Venn diagram with three circles,
and connecting point, and I'm at the center of it.
And those circles are tech, user experience, and business strategic planning.
So when I discovered about ITK, it's like, okay,
here's an avenue that helps me explore those interests.
It's an avenue that shows cross-cut in thinking and applying it to problem-solving.
So that was kind of the journey there.
In fact, I didn't hear about ITK until I found, like, a comic book,
or a comic strip that Dan created.
It was something about building a cake, and he's using it as an analogy for innovation.
And I just reached out to him and said, "You know, I read this comic here."
I found it interesting, because at the time, I was reading a book about using comic books,
or the art of drawing comics, to explain an idea.
And so, I found that very interesting.
So that just kind of showed a level of creativity, and kind of thinking differently,
that I didn't see anywhere else in MITRE.
And when you touched on it, I didn't see -- even though I described it as a day job, geospatial
or -- I even refer to myself more as a geographer than a geospatial analyst.
It's not -- I don't see this group facilitation effort as a departure from that background.
It's more of an extension, in that even geography --
I mentioned that Venn diagram before, with user experience,
tech, and business strategic planning.
Geography's also broad.
So you can consider other Venn diagrams there.
There's human geography.
There's, you know, about human interaction with the environment.
There's physical geography about the Earth's physical features, and its atmosphere.
And then there's also that technological side of geography, which is the GIS,
and the satellite imagery and whatnot.
And you think about how those three things need to intersect in order for you to solve problems,
to consider a problem like climate change or land use.
And you can see how that can be at the center of that Venn diagram.
So again, the beauty of these tools is that cross-cut in thinking,
that kind of encouraging you to focus on the problem,
as Tracey mentioned, as a starting point.
And, you know, from there, you can generate ideas.
You can build a team.
You can develop hypotheses, explore evidence, infuse knowledge together.
So that's been my journey so far.
>> Wonderful, thank you so much, Karim, for walking us through that,
and the visual of the Venn diagram also helps.
It reminds me a little bit of the Ikigai, finding your passion,
and what you're good at, the Ikigai chart.
I don't know if you're familiar with that.
It's a four-part Venn diagram that -- it's a Japanese term, Ikigai, finding your passion,
and what it is that you're good at.
So very much along those lines, and I love the fact
that you all bring these different perspectives.
And it's incredible, because we talk about innovation and innovative teams
that bring a diversity and perspective.
And we see this here, because I'm learning so much.
And we've been talking for about half an hour, and I've learned so much in the last 30 minutes
from the different perspectives, and how you all have come together.
And I love the fact that you reached out to Dan
because you saw this baking a cake comic that he put together.
And we asked him -- I had no idea.
We asked Dan to put that in the chat.
So thank you very much, Karim.
I think we'll come back and chat some more, but this helps us segue to Josh,
who is a future strategic designer.
And he also bridges data-driven and human-driven innovation,
and Karim sort of set the stage there.
Because he's looking at data from a geospatial perspective, and putting the innovator
or the -- and the problem in the core.
So Josh, how do you then take data-driven --
how do you bridge the data-driven and the human-driven elements to innovate?
Josh, over to you.
>> Yeah, absolutely.
Thank you for the question.
It's something I've been thinking about for some time.
So before I came to MITRE, I worked as a data analyst for a startup for some time,
and I went back to grad school, where I studied design
and transition design, thinking about the future.
And throughout that journey, that unexpected journey and kind of winding journey
like Casey talked about, what I've come to see for myself and in teams I've worked with is
that really to bridge the data and human needs, we as innovators and as teams looking
to create impact and novelty, as Karim talked about, need to hit pause a little bit
on the idea that data-driven development is the gold standard for innovation.
Data-driven work is really good at showing impact, and is really steeped in the sciences,
but it misses what the human need is.
So like what Casey talked about, if you're crossing a creek by a raging river,
do you need a bed and breakfast, or do you need extra tools there, right?
Which might be the novelty, or experience that you gain along the way.
If we're only to focus on data-driven ideas,
we tend to end up with the next model smartphone, which is really great.
I think we can all appreciate it, and we want to upgrade our phones every few years,
and brings a lot of value to our life.
And if you only focus on the human need, you may end up with a warehouse full of fidget spinners,
which they may be great, but they tend to be just entertainment.
For me, bridging those devices are using tools,
such as innovation toolkit, to -- another Venn diagram.
If you were to layer, like, the data side of needs, and that human side over together,
of impact and novelty, novelty from the human side, where those overlap is
where the area for innovation is ripe.
And it's important -- you asked how you bridge it -- is to use some sort of tool,
and safe space to bring individuals from kind of the anthropological side of understanding
or social sciences, and the engineering side together in the same room,
to help define the problem, discuss the pre mortems, do all of those meaningful things.
So that you get the diverse perspectives that bring meaning
and truly lead to that innovation and impact.
And so, for me as a strategist in the design strategy,
what I like to do is bring those groups together, and then get them thinking about not,
like, what is the problem today, but what does that look like in 10 years, or 20 years.
And set a vision or goal that may seem audacious, or loose guide, third horizon,
like we don't know, but it gives that motivation to start the journey down that path,
and have those meaningful conversations around what is possible.
>> Wonderful.
Thank you so much, Josh.
And thank you for referencing and connecting all the way back to the visual
that Casey provided for us, which was the river.
Because, Casey, we're coming back to you again, and as the conversation evolves, I'm hearing --
of course, we're talking about the tools, but we also have the responsibility
to motivate innovators, to -- or motivate the team to think differently.
